articles.title: Arrests made in Mohamed Al Fayed probe in France, police say
articles.summary: The Ritz hotel in Paris, which is still owned by the Al Fayed family, is one of the properties searched by police.
body: Hundreds of women have come forward with abuse allegations against the former Harrods and Ritz Paris owner
French police have made arrests after three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, were searched in relation to an investigation into Mohamed Al Fayed's abuse.
The Paris prosecutor's office told the BBC that several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released.

In a confidential letter sent to survivors, the Metropolitan Police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in what is understood to be a joint operation between British and French authorities.
It is the first time any arrests have been made in relation to alleged abuse and trafficking by the former Harrods and Ritz owner.
Mohamed Al Fayed accused of multiple rapes by staff
Several victims of Al Fayed were also interviewed by French investigators, the prosecutor's office said.

It added that the searches were part of a preliminary investigation into "allegations of human trafficking committed by an organized group, aggravated pimping committed by an organized group, and rape".
The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed.
The late Egyptian billionaire bought the Ritz Paris hotel in 1979, and it is still owned by the Al Fayed family.

The Villa Windsor in western Paris, another property involved in the search, was a holiday home for the Al Fayed family. It was previously the home of King Edward VIII, following his abdication, and his wife Wallis Simpson.
The Met shared this statement from French authorities with victims:
"At this stage of the proceedings, several victims have been interviewed by French investigators, and the investigations are being conducted in liaison with the British authorities.

"In this context, searches and evidence-gathering operations were carried out in mid-October 2026, notably within the Hotel Ritz in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, as well as at the Villa Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez, a former property of Mohamed Al Fayed, and at the Villa Windsor in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, in the presence of British investigators.

"Several suspects were taken into police custody, measures which were lifted following their interviews, specifically for the purpose of analyzing digital material seized during the search operations.
"The investigations are continuing under the direction of the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office."
A Met Police spokesperson confirmed its officers travelled to France in October and were present during the operation.
The Ritz hotel in Paris is still owned by the Al Fayed family
Al Fayed, who died in 2023 aged 94, was accused by more than 20 women of sexual assault in a BBC documentary and podcast in September 2024.
One of the women featured in the documentary said she was sexually assaulted by Al Fayed at the Ritz hotel in Paris, while another woman said she had been raped by him at the Villa Windsor residence.
Since those allegations, more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers.
A woman has also told BBC Scotland she was trafficked, drugged, sexually assaulted and held prisoner on the Balnagown Estate by Al Fayed's brother, Salah Fayed, who died in 2010.
Both brothers died without facing legal charges in relation to these allegations.
Earlier this year, Police Scotland said it was carrying out further investigations into allegations connected to Balnagown Estate.
In a statement, a force spokesperson said: "Three people have been identified in connection with offending against a number of victims.
"Our inquiries are ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further."
The Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors group said it welcomed the "significant developments" and cooperation between the Met and French authorities.

"We believe that all properties owned by Fayed should be investigated with the same thoroughness as those already searched, wherever they are located, to ensure that no potentially relevant evidence is overlooked," the group said.
"We hope these developments represent meaningful progress towards identifying and holding to account all those who facilitated, concealed or assisted his offending, wherever they operated."

The survivor advocacy group No One Above said: "France is treating this as organised human trafficking, led by specialists, with properties searched and evidence seized. That is what a serious investigation into a network looks like.
"Two years on, survivors are still waiting for the same from the Met. It is time the National Crime Agency took this investigation over."

The management of the Ritz Paris told AFP news agency that it "does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour" and that it was ready "to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities".
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in Oviedo
articles.summary: Officers attended the scene in connection with a separate incident at a residential building in the city.
body: A police officer has died and another has been injured in the northern Spanish city of Oviedo after an explosive device went off at the scene of a shooting.
The blast happened when officers from Spain's canine unit and explosives disposal unit arrived and examined a suspicious backpack following reports of a dispute between neighbours on Tuesday morning.
A woman who had been shot and the injured officer have been taken to hospital for treatment.
The suspect fled the scene and is still at large, police said.
Spanish police paid tribute to the dead officer, who has been named as Juan José, in a statement on X and said: "Our hearts are with his family, friends, colleagues and loved ones."
Officers attended the scene early after receiving reports of an argument between neighbours and upon arriving found a woman who had sustained gunshot wounds, police spokesman Pedro Aguado said.
While searching for the suspected attacker, officers found a suspicious backpack with a flashing light and contacted both the bomb disposal unit and canine unit.
"While the package was being moved outside to ensure the safety of the residents, an explosion occurred," Aguado added.
The explosion left a member of the canine unit dead and an officer from the bomb disposal unit seriously injured, he said.
A three-year-old police dog named Deny was also killed in the explosion.
A widespread police operation is ongoing near the scene of the explosion and officers are continuing to hunt for the suspect.
Taking to social media, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was "deeply shocked" by the fatal incident and paid tribute to the officer injured in the explosion.
"Your dedication and courage deserve the gratitude of an entire country," he said.
Spanish opposition leader and President of the People's Party Alberto Núñez Feijóo said: "What happened in Oviedo is heartbreaking.
"My condolences to the family of the officer who died and my best wishes for the recovery of the one who was seriously injured.

articles.title: DR Congo sentences 66 soldiers to death for being 'cowards'
articles.summary: The Congolese army's fight against rebel groups has long been hampered by disarray within its ranks.
body: The Congolese army has been fighting rebels for decades
At least 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in the Democratic Republic of Congo for cowardice, mutiny and refusing to obey orders, local media report.

The sentences followed a trial of 71 soldiers before a military court in Walikale, in North Kivu province, in eastern DR Congo. Four soldiers were acquitted, while another was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
The army said the trial was intended to improve discipline among troops as they battle armed groups in eastern DR Congo.
The region has endured decades of conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition that includes the M23 group.
The soldiers were reportedly arrested on 20 October in Walikale, where they were accused of abandoning their positions and fleeing during clashes with FRN fighters.
The Congolese army's campaign against armed groups, including the M23, has long been undermined by poor discipline and disorganisation within its ranks.
The government has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda of supporting the M23, an allegation denied by both Kigali and the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
The army has faced persistent criticism over its lack of professionalism and disciplined, while soldiers have complained of poor pay and inadequate equipment.
Last month, another 27 soldiers were sentenced to death on similar charges of cowardice after reportedly withdrawing from the frontline during clashes with rebels.
In March 2024, DR Congo lifted a 20-year moratorium on the death penalty, citing the need to remove "traitors" within the army.
The government said capital punishment would also apply to people involved in armed groups, insurrection, as well as committing treason and war crimes.
The decision to reinstate the death penalty was widely criticised by rights groups. However, no formal executions have been carried out since the moratorium was lifted.
Since the beginning of 2025, at least 507 soldiers have been convicted, including 381 death sentences, according to figures compiled by French broadcaster RFI.

In October 2025, former Congolese President Joseph Kabila was sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself. He has since been named as the FRN's leader.

articles.title: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
articles.summary: The Odyssey was meant to take guests around the world for years, but the trip was cut short after its operator ran out of money.
body: The arrest comes weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end, leaving 200 guests stranded in Cambodia
A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.
The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.

Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".
The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.
"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".
Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.
The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.

Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.
"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.
However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.

While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.

CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.
It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.
Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.

As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.
It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

articles.title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: The US president said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about the affair with the alleged spy.
body: "He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.
"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.
Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off its value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.

Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the investigation, or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.
According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.

The American firm, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating Nvidia's exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.
Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.
The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.
At the White House, Trump was asked several times, including by the BBC, when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.
Trump said he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.
"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.

He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".
Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.
The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.
He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.
Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear.

A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".
Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.
Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.
Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.
It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.
Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.

articles.title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.summary: Tons of chilled and frozen food was spoiled last month as fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets heated up.
body: Fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France were affected last month
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.
Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions.
Iran has yet to respond officially, but some Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless.

The French hacking, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen anc chilled food in France was followed by a similar attack against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.

Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.

In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
If the IRGC carried out the cyber-attacks, it remains unclear whether they were part of Iran's deterrence strategy.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.

More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

articles.title: California police investigate after 27 fall ill at half-marathon running event
articles.summary: A local hospital says runners had "unusual" symptoms after racing on an atypically hot day.
body: Thousands took part in the event on a hotter-than-usual day in Santa Barbara
Police in Santa Barbara, California, are investigating after nearly 30 people had to seek medical care at a half-marathon running event held in the city on Sunday.

In a statement provided to the BBC's US partner CBS News, officers said they received a report from Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital about race participants who sought medical treatment "for unusual symptoms" after the race ended.
"The cause of the reported symptoms has not been confirmed," the statement added.
Cottage Health, which operates the hospital, told CBS it had seen "a larger than expected number of emergency visits" from those who ran the race.

"There is no specific action recommended for the public at this time; however, participants who feel unwell should seek medical attention and follow guidance from healthcare professionals," police said.
Cottage Hospital said it treated 27 people from the half marathon at emergency rooms in Santa Barbara and the nearby city of Goleta.
The vast majority of them - 24 - were discharged after treatment, while three people were still in hospital as of Monday in stable condition.

Several thousand people ran the half marathon on a hotter-than-usual day in Santa Barbara along the Pacific Ocean. Temperatures reportedly reached 86F (27C) by midday, compared to a typical early November temperature of low 70s.
One of the runners who went to hospital told local news outlet KEYT-TV that they had lost consciousness and could not remember parts of the race.
"It is awfully suspicious," said the runner, who declined to be identified. "We had people saying they were hallucinating."
"I am not too familiar with heat exhaustion but I have never seen anyone not remembering a long portion of their run," the runner added.
Event director David Monico told US media that 15 people were taken from the medical tent to local hospitals because of dehydration and overheating.
The BBC has contacted the Santa Barbara Police Department, Cottage Health and the half marathon organisers for further comment.

articles.title: Israeli forces kill Palestinian boy in West Bank, health ministry says
articles.summary: The Israeli military says its soldiers opened fire at individuals “who intended to hurl stones” at a road used by Israelis.
body: Israeli forces carried out a raid in the Old City of Nablus, near Burqa, on Sunday
Israeli forces have shot dead a 14-year-old Palestinian boy during an operation in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say.
Moataz Daghlas was killed on Monday evening in the village of Burqa, north-west of Nablus, according to the Palestinian health ministry.

The Israeli military said soldiers identified "several terrorists who intended to hurl stones" in an area where stones had previously been thrown at Israeli vehicles. The soldiers fired towards them "to remove the threat", it added.
The Palestinian Red Crescent said its teams treated two people with gunshot wounds, but that Israeli forces blocked their access to a third wounded person and detained three volunteer paramedics.
Moataz Daghlas's relatives said Israeli authorities were withholding his body.

Meanwhile, Palestinian news agency Wafa identified the two Palestinians wounded during the raid as a 17-year-old child, who it said was shot in the abdomen and pelvis, and a 19-year-old man, who was shot in the hand.
According to the UN, at least 98 Palestinians, including 22 children, have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year.
Six Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, it says.

The rules of engagement for Israeli forces were reportedly broadened after the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, allowing soldiers increased discretion to use lethal force against a perceived threat.

In June, the UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory said it had verified the killing of 241 Palestinian children by Israeli security forces and settlers in the West Bank since then.
Most of the children were teenage boys and, in many cases, Israeli authorities accused them of having engaged in stone-throwing as justification, it found.

The UN office said its assessment was that none of the children killed while involved in confrontations with Israeli forces had posed an imminent threat to life, which it said was the only legal justification for the use of lethal force in the West Bank under international law.

articles.title: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
articles.summary: The president says the US is keeping "status quo" with Iran but remains “locked and loaded” should the situation change.
body: Trump: "Iran militarily is effectively over"
Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.
"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."
Trump's comments came after he met the Qatari prime minister. Qatar is a US ally in the Gulf region, and one of Iran's neighbours, which has been a key mediator in efforts to end the war.
Addressing reporters in the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.
Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.
This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.

The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.

Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.
Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.
"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.
Global oil prices, which have fallen sharply since the midterms, dipped further after Trump's comments.
On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude was more than 1% lower at $91.50 (£52) while US-traded was down by 1.2% at $85.82.
Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?
Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.
In a post on X, the Qatari leader said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".
Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.

Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to the threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.
Republican congressman Thomas Massie plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth
Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.

Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.
Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".

While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

articles.title: Oxford museum returns ancestral Naga skulls to India
articles.summary: The remains will be taken to Nagaland, where tribal leaders plan a joint memorial and burial.
body: A delegation of 30 people had travelled to Oxford from India's Nagaland
The University of Oxford has returned the remains of 39 people taken from the Naga community during British colonial rule in India.
A delegation of around 30 people from Nagaland, a mountainous state in north-eastern India, attended a ceremony at Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum on Monday to mark the handover.

The remains, most of which are skulls, will be taken back to India and given what Naga tribal leaders have described as a "respectful rest". There are plans to bury them under a joint memorial in a park in Nagaland.
Museum director Laura Van Broekhoven described it as "a historic moment that will be part of stories told to next generations".
She said the remains were finally on their way home after overcoming "so much red tape everywhere".
The human remains were displayed at the Oxford museum for decades before being removed from public view in 2020 as part of what it described as a "decolonisation process".
The museum formally handed over the remains and signed an agreement with Naga leaders on Monday

The Pitt Rivers Museum holds more than 6,000 objects associated with Naga culture, believed to be the largest such collection in the world. Most were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar (the former Burma).
The museum's website lists 219 items as human remains.
These were added to the museum's collection between 1910 and 1940 and mostly collected by two colonial administrators who were anthropologists.
The museum's website, external mentions that the objects collected during this period were "frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given".
During their visit to Oxford, the Naga delegation also met descendants of one of the anthropologists involved in collecting the remains.
"The manner in which these human remains were taken away from our land leaves much for us to speculate," one of the tribal leaders, Thejao Vihienuo, told AFP.
"I suspect that nobody would have given the skull of his father or his grandfather as a gift to another person."
Anthropologists say that the Naga people once practised head hunting, severing the heads of enemies as trophies. But they also kept the heads of their own chiefs at the centre of villages.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, founded in the 19th Century, has previously returned human remains to indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand and the US.
The latest handover to India concerns only the 39 ancestral remains and comes after a visit by a Naga delegation to Oxford in 2025, when it formally requested their return.
The museum had announced in September that the remains would be returned to India.

articles.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
articles.summary: AI safety regulator will also be created after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked government websites.
body: PM Anthony Albanese says the law needs to catch up with a "fast-changing world"
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

articles.title: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
articles.summary: The Australian airline said the move was aimed at modernising its IT systems and noted the impact of AI.
body: Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson apologised for the "hard news" of 850 job cuts
Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.
In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".

The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.
Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.
The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.
On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".
Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.
"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.

The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".
The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".
Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.
Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.
The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

articles.title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 16 people
articles.summary: Eyewitnesses say the explosion shook the ground, with one believing an earthquake had hit near the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.
body: A fire broke out at the factory following the explosion which some eyewitnesses confused with an earthquake
At least 16 people have died and 13 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.

All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas plant, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.
The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.
Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.
Eyewitnesses said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.
In a statement, the company said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.
Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people are believed to be still under the rubble.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued. He also said two of the injured were in a serious condition.
At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.
The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

articles.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
articles.summary: The ruling means the case can move forward, possibly with reduced charges in a new trial.
body: The BBC's Ione Wells on how the Lindsay Clancy trial gripped America - and ultimately fell apart
A Massachusetts judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of killing her three children.
The judge's ruling follows her defence team's request to dismiss the case after the 12-person jury in her September trial failed to reach a verdict.
Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.
Clancy's defence team argued to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that prevents a person from being tried for the same crime twice.

Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the 26-day jury trial last summer, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative.
The five-week trial, its lead-up and aftermath gripped Americans, and put postpartum mental health issues such as psychosis in the spotlight.
In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject Clancy to double jeopardy, according to court documents obtained by the BBC.
The possibility that "an unreasonably stubborn or eccentric juror" could be seated is "an unavoidable risk of the jury system", he said.

"Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy."
Sullivan also denied a defence motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath.
He said the defence failed to demonstrate that the records were needed for Clancy's defence at any retrial, and that questioning the juror "would have been impermissibly coercive".
The judge has marked 16 November to discuss scheduling a potential second trial. He previously suggested it could begin in March.
The BBC has contacted Clancy's lawyers for comment.
Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband says he forgave her so he would not be 'eaten up inside forever'
Lindsay Clancy's trial puts postpartum psychosis in the spotlight

Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.
After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict.
The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity.
In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant.

Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty.
Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.
Ana Faguy contributed reporting.

articles.title: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk killer set for June 2028
articles.summary: Tyler Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the 2025 killing of the conservative activist.
body: Kirk was a prominent conservative youth activist
The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered.
Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the September 2025 killing of Kirk, 31, who was shot while he spoke at a Utah college campus.

Utah County judge Tony Graf Jr on Monday told the court that jury selection would begin on 21 June, 2028. The prosecution has estimated the trial could last 17 weeks, while defence lawyers have said it could take seven months.
Robinson could face the death penalty if found guilty of aggravated murder, something his defence team has sought to prevent.
Prosecutors previously told the court they could be ready for trial by October 2027 but were willing to move that date back to January 2028 to avoid the holiday period.

But defence attorneys said they needed more time to prepare their case and floated a 2029 start. As well as trying to stop Robinson facing the death penalty, they have also tried to have cameras banned from the courtroom.

Kirk's widow, Erika, with whom he had two children, had pushed for as early a trial date as possible while also arguing proceedings should be live-streamed. She, along with Kirk's parents, ⁠Robert and Kathryn, have attended a number of court hearings in the case.
Robinson's legal team is trying to get the death penalty taken off the table in his trial

At the end of Monday's proceedings, Erica Kirk's lawyer, Jeffrey A Nieman, told the judge that while "a trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family", they had "no choice but obviously to accept the schedule the court's put forward".
Nieman added: "The family has waited long enough already; they should not have to wait any longer for this."
During a five-day preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.

This included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.
"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court in September.

"We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.
Defence attorneys, meanwhile, have cast doubt upon evidence and expert witness credentials in the case.
Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial

articles.title: Inside devastated front-line city that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
articles.summary: The BBC gains rare access to a specialist drone unit defending the eastern city of Slovyansk from heavy Russian fire.
body: Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting devastated front-line city
The dangers in Slovyansk are clear from the start.
"If I say run, you run," Tetiana tells us. She and her colleague Yasha are escorting us into a city now under constant bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.
It is raining and cloudy as we enter the city, and our military escorts call this "good" weather, meaning it is bad for drones.
But the threat is still there, and Yasha keeps his eyes peeled on the skies, while 21-year-old Tetiana scours her phone for the latest military intelligence on likely threats from the air.
They are members of a drone unit who call themselves Peaky Blinders and their distinctive emblem is a flat cap of the type made popular by the cult BBC TV series, although theirs are camouflaged.
Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.
Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.
Ukrainians worry that doing so would make it much easier for Russia to advance further west, including to the capital Kyiv.
Very little of the city has been left unscathed by months of heavy bombardment

Once inside the city, we leave our vehicles hidden under the cover of trees and venture out on foot. Yasha carries a shotgun – a last resort to shoot down Russian drones. In halting English, Tetiana tells us walking is safer than travelling by car.
Abandoned vehicles litter the streets – recently destroyed by remotely operated Russian first-person view drones. The anti-drone netting that covers the roads is no guarantee of safety.
Tetiana shows us a video on her phone taken a few days earlier.

You can hear several drones buzzing above her, and then the cacophony of small arms fire as Ukrainian forces try to shoot them down. Tetiana admits it can be scary but explains how she felt compelled to help her country, abandoning her dreams of becoming an opera singer.
Slovyansk is now a husk of its former self. Very few buildings have been left unscathed, with many reduced to rubble.

Tetiana shows us a school recently destroyed by Russian glide bombs. Across the road there is a gaping hole in an abandoned residential block. Broken glass litters the pavement. The few shops still functioning are boarded up – making it hard to distinguish what is still open. Most have closed.

Tetiana says the Russians are doing everything they can to intimidate people and drive them out of the city. That, she says, "is their strategy – to make people leave in chaos, gathering up their last belongings and fleeing amid enormous fear and suffering. They want people to have nowhere left to live".

It is a familiar pattern already seen in other Ukrainian towns and cities in the Donbas – like Pokrovsk and Bakhmut. These are now ghost towns reduced to rubble, but eventually falling into Russian hands.
Russia has already taken nearly 90% of the Donbas – made up of the regions of Luhansk and Donetsk - but its advances this year have all but stalled in the face of strong Ukrainian resistance.
The White House is sounding positive about the revived talks in Abu Dhabi, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's refusal to cede the territory.

October was the deadliest month for Russian troops since the start of its full-scale invasion – with more than 54,000 killed or injured, according to Ukraine's general staff. Despite this, Russian forces are still making life in the Fortress Belt cities almost impossible.
Iryna, who works in one of the city's last remaining cafes, is one of the few residents who decided to stay
Before the war, Slovyansk was a city of more than 200,000 people. Less than 10% of those remain and the population diminishes by the day.

But amid the wail of near constant air raid warnings, there are still signs of people clinging on to life here. Iryna works in one of the city's last remaining coffee shops. Slovyansk is where she was born.
"I'm forced to walk around crying," she tells me. "How can they do this?"
Life, she says, has become incredibly difficult. She has already lost her house. But despite her tears, there is still defiance: "I won't leave Slovyansk. This is my home."
Inga, 53, was also born and raised here and continues to work in the city despite the danger.
"It's stressful. Honestly, I don't even know what to say," she says, but she is staying because of what she calls the "fear of the unknown".
"I simply have nowhere to go, and I don't have the money to leave or support myself afterwards." Nor, she says, is there anywhere else in Ukraine she would consider truly safe.
Commander Oleksandr of the Peaky Blinders special forces unit says neither side is able to advance because of the large number of drones in use
We first met the Omega National Guard Special Forces drone unit two years ago fighting in the Kharkiv region, in north-eastern Ukraine.
Just four of the original team remain - the rest have moved to other units, or they have been wounded or killed.
Among the dead was the brother of the man in charge of the unit, Oleksandr, who now describes his unit as his family.
He jokes it is just like the Peaky Blinders TV show – "but without the crime and the drugs". Back at their base they share a meal every evening.

Oleksandr reads out a prayer of thanks for surviving another day – he says it strengthens their spirits. The meal is accompanied by classical music played on a speaker. It helps drown out the noise of the explosions nearby.
"I feel this is the most difficult situation we've ever faced," says Oleksandr, who underlines the importance of holding the line.

"We must be here to inflict maximum damage on the enemy. We're fighting here because this is where the most intense phase of the war is taking place. Russia's claim that they will reach the borders of the Donbas, seize it, and then the war will end is absolutely false," he insists.

The remaining fortress belt cities provide Ukraine with a strong defensive line and are a major obstacle to any Russian advance. The saturation of drones in the area is also now making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance here.
Peace talks may have resumed, but Oleksandr notes they have not led to anything so far.
"I really want this war to end," he says, "but do I believe these negotiations will succeed? No, I don't really believe they will".
The streets are largely empty, with increasing numbers of residents evacuated as drone attacks intensify
The next morning we are not the only ones making an exit. A dozen civilians have arrived at an evacuation point in the centre to be escorted out.
They hold all the belongings they can carry and are taken into a bunker for their safety. Outside there is another heavy blast of small arms fire, signalling more drones are nearby.

Alina Shyrko, herself a resident of Slovyansk, is co-ordinating the move of civilians out of the city and says the situation has deteriorated rapidly over the past few months. Families with children have already been ordered to leave.
"Everyone is thinking about leaving," she says, "I'm thinking about it too."
Ukraine still holds Slovyansk but its lifeblood, its people, are ebbing away.
Additional reporting by Rebecca Hartmann and Volodymyr Lozhko.

articles.title: Polish unity on show as thousands join silent march for Krakow shooting victims
articles.summary: Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by Saturday's attack, writes Sarah Rainsford.
body: Thousands gathered at Krakow's historic Market Square to honour the victims of Saturday's attack
Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend.
The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times.
As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower.
Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, each one marking a spot where someone died.
Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened.
The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.
Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday.

Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it is too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology.

"The minister wanted to win domestic political points. That's not responsible behaviour," Pawel Musialek of the Jagiellonian University suggests, in a country where politics is highly - and often viciously - polarised.
"So far we've seen no clear message that this guy was strongly ideological, and that it's not more like something from the darknet."

There has been no mention of any letter or manifesto that Oksinski left. One neighbour told Polish news site Onet that the 24-year-old was a "bit of a loner" but few who knew him well have spoken publicly.
What we know so far after Krakow gun attack
In addition to his electronic devices like his phone, investigators are examining a number of badges that Oksinski had attached to his military-style outfit.

The prosecutor's office says a yellow Gadsden flag with a coiled snake symbol was displayed in his bedroom. "It has various meanings of freedom and rebellion," a spokesman emphasised. "Not necessarily negative."
It was at Oksinski's home that the bodies of his parents and sister were discovered.
It is alleged that he shot them, before driving some 200km (125 miles) south to continue the killing in Krakow.
Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died
Two days on, shops and cafes around the market square are beginning to fill up again, but the mood is subdued.
A Zara clothes shop is still boarded up, after bullets smashed the glass. A local man in his 50s died just outside.
Jo, a Scottish tourist, saw paramedics "who got there ridiculously fast", fighting to save him. "It was all pretty grim."
Like many, she initially mistook the rifle shots for fireworks.
On the opposite corner of the square, beside another cluster of flowers, people keep pausing to take pictures of the holes that were blasted into the wall by gunfire.
One of the six victims has been identified as a Polish painter in her 50s, who was a mother of four, and in town with friends for an exhibition opening.
A British citizen and an Austrian who died are yet to be named publicly.
Several drivers of the horse-drawn carriages that are usually poised to trot tourists around the square were seriously injured.
Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion
Olha, who works in a nearby chocolate shop says everyone is now nervous.
On Saturday, people rushed into her store to escape the gunman who was tearing around in his car, firing through the window.
Olha is Ukrainian, and moved to Krakow when Russia invaded. "We left our own country for safety. This is supposed to be a safe place!" she said.
"It's so sad, and so scary. Especially that he drove all the way here for two hours, planning this and thinking about it."
She regrets that the gunman did not survive: "So many are dead, so many lives have been ruined, and now there will be no justice."
Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday
When Oksinski's car was searched, four firearms and "hundreds of rounds of ammunition" were found, all owned legally by the alleged killer and his father.
Both were members of the Swit Starachowice sports club, where there is a shooting range. A spokesman recalls Michal Oksinski as unremarkable: average competition results and normal behaviour.
He had been just three times this year, most recently in August with his father. The club spokesman is adamant that it does not train combat firing, only shooting from a fixed point.
Gun ownership in Poland has grown considerably since war broke out in Ukraine just across the border, but this is the first mass shooting anyone here can remember.
Inevitably, it has brought scrutiny of the checks over who qualifies to handle such weapons, including psychological tests, as Michal Oksinski passed all of them.
On Monday, the government announced an urgent review.
"Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"
At the spot where Oksinski's car was intercepted and he was shot by police there is another memorial, this one in honour of the officers still in hospital.
Some have brought flowers, but a girl called Bianka has left a card that reads: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon."
A couple of steps away, there's a series of bullet holes in the glass.
"This man was a real hero, he didn't hesitate," Ania says, referring to officer Jakub Kulik who was shot in the chest. His condition remains serious. "We're here to help him fight for his life."
"Nothing like this has never happened before, it's terrible," a young man called Wojtek tells me.
He's only glad that the gunman responsible for such horror turned out to be Polish.
"People here are already against immigration, so that would have been even worse."
Ania thinks Poles will pull through, though the country's image as a low-crime oasis has been shattered.
Most of all, she's angry that Michal Oksinski died without being held to account for the devastation.
"I think we deserve to know why."

articles.title: Activist wins 10-year fight against homophobic Trinidad and Tobago laws
articles.summary: Jason Jones welcomes decision by privy council in London to overturn 2025 ruling that outlawed anal sex
body: A gay man has won a historic 10-year battle against Trinidad and Tobago’s homophobic laws with a landmark UK appeals court ruling that could help overturn similar anti-gay laws in other Caribbean countries.

The privy council, based in London, overturned a 2025 decision by Trinidad and Tobago’s court of appeal that recriminalised consensual anal sex, seven years after the Trinidadian activist Jason Jones secured a high court judgment declaring the country’s colonial-era “buggery” laws unconstitutional.
In explaining its ruling on Tuesday, the court said: “The ability to form a deep connection with another person through an intimate and loving relationship is a vital interest for all human beings.”
“This judgment will have a domino effect across every country that has the privy council as its supreme court. It will change many millions of people’s lives,” Jones said in a statement.
“I’m looking forward to going home, switching off everything and living with this moment for a while.”

Jones’ lawyer Caroline Edwards hailed Tuesday’s unanimous victory as “an emphatic victory for Jason, for all gay men and women in Trinidad and Tobago and for all people who believe in the fundamental rights of everyone.”

Reflecting on the case’s long journey, she said: “All judges who heard the case in Trinidad and Tobago were unanimous that the 1986 legislation was not justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for rights and freedoms, and all the privy council judges agreed.”

The privy council is the final court of appeal for Trinidad and Tobago and several other Commonwealth countries, giving the ruling potentially far-reaching significance for other Caribbean jurisdictions where similar laws remain in force.

Jones has been fighting the “buggery law”, whose origins date to British colonial rule, for a decade. In a historic 2018 victory, high court judge Devindra Rampersad ruled that the provisions criminalising consensual anal sex were unconstitutional. But the government appealed, and in 2025 the court of appeal overturned that decision.

Tuesday’s privy council decision restores Jones’s victory, with all five judges finding that sections 13 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act 1986 must be interpreted consistently with the constitution so that they do not criminalise private, consensual sexual relations between adults of the same sex.

It marks the latest significant advance for LGBTQ+ rights in the Caribbean, after a landmark ruling in St Lucia last year, when the Eastern Caribbean supreme court struck down colonial-era laws criminalising consensual gay sex.

Asked whether this would make Jones, who has lived in London for several decades, feel comfortable living in Trinidad again, he said no. “The thing about liberation movements is every time you move the needle forward, you get the pushback. I got a lot of pushback from the queer community [in Trinidad] saying: ‘Don’t stir the pot.’ But you have to. I’m not afraid of pushback.”
